newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Fourth letter bomb found at U.N. headquarters.
newsitem.headline: Fourth letter bomb found at U.N. headquarters.

text.p: U.N. security staff found a fourth letter bomb early on Tuesday sent to the U.N. bureau of an Arabic-language newspaper, a day after a letter bomb exploded at the paper's London office.
Security sources said all four letter bombs uncovered at the United Nations were addressed to the U.N. bureau of the Saudi-owned Al-Hayat newspaper, which is based in London.
They were defused by the New York City police bomb squad, which was summoned to U.N. headquarters.
No one was injured in New York. The bomb that exploded early on Monday in London wounded two security guards. Four more suspected devices were subsequently found there, British police said.

U.N. personnel were working around the clock, searching at least 40,000 parcels and letters that had accumulated over the weekend. Great piles of mail were taken to an area near the U.N. General Assembly hall so a second electronic scanner, usually reserved for tourists, could be put to use.
Outside the U.N. headquarters on Manhattan's East River, New York police stood guard and fire engines arrived periodically.

The letter bombs were contained in greeting card-sized envelopes. The first was found about 11 a.m. (1600 GMT) on Monday in a second-floor messenger room, about 15 minutes before it would have been delivered, U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said. The second one was discovered in the main mail room in the basement several hours later.

They were addressed to the Al-Hayat's bureau, not to any specific individual. U.N. security was on the lookout for mail addressed to Al-Hayat after its U.N. correspondent, Raghida Dergham, informed them of the London incident.
After the first suspicious envelope was found, parts of two floors of the 38-floor complex were closed and part of the press area was evacuated.
The third letter bomb was discovered late on Monday and like the two previous ones, was addressed to Al-Hayat.

The letters at the United Nations were similar to five mailed earlier this month to the newspaper's Washington bureau. U.N. sources said the letters, like those received in Washington, bore an Alexandria, Egypt, postmark.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation launched an investigation earlier this month after eight letter bombs made to look like Christmas cards were mailed from Egypt to the United States.
Four arrived at Al-Hayat's Washington office and a fifth was found in the mail system. Three other devices turned up in the area around Leavenworth federal prison in Kansas.

Mohammad Salameh, a militant Moslem jailed for life for the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, is in Leavenworth, as are Victor Alvarez and Mohammed Saleh who were convicted of plotting to blow up U.N. headquarters and other targets.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan told reporters late on Monday that "We consider it an attack on the organisation and also on freedom of press and speech. We hope that whoever has undertaken this cowardly act will cease before some serious damage is done."

"This is a house of peace and we work in the interest of all nations," he said, adding "This kind of activity is not something that anyone can condone and I appeal to them to desist and use other means to raise their complaints."
